Does the city shape how our brain handles stress?

Living in a city and growing up in one leave different traces in the brain’s response to social stress.

More than half of humanity lives in cities. Cities offer opportunity, yet urban living has also been linked to a higher risk of anxiety and mood disorders. Where in the brain could this connection begin?

The study

Researchers in Mannheim used functional MRI while healthy volunteers solved tasks under social stress. They compared people living in cities, towns and the countryside, and people who had grown up in more or less urban surroundings. The main results were confirmed in further experiments with a different stress task and a new group of participants.

The findings

Current city living was associated with stronger activity in the amygdala, a region involved in threat and emotion. It was lowest in people from the countryside, higher in town dwellers and highest in city dwellers. Growing up in a city was associated with activity in the perigenual anterior cingulate cortex, a region that helps to regulate the amygdala and stress. The study shows associations, not causes.

What this means for architecture

If urban environments shape how we process social stress, then density, noise, places of retreat and public spaces that allow calm encounters become questions of mental health as much as of design.

Conclusion

The city does not only surround us. It may also shape how our brain responds to stress.

Lederbogen et al. (2011)

City living and urban upbringing affect neural social stress processing in humans. Nature, 474(7352), 498-501.
